cases.text: President Andrew Johnson vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau Bill in February 1866, arguing it would extend military jurisdiction over civilians in peacetime and let agents act as judges without juries in states that had no representation in Congress. That shows the Bureau was seen as intruding into Southern civil life, which is Dunning's point about its intrusion and the opposition it met.

In May 1867, after the Military Reconstruction Acts, Bureau Circular No. 9 told Bureau officers to inform freedmen when and where to register and to disregard threats. White Southerners who saw federal agents backing Black voting could regard the Bureau as an instrument of national control over the South, as Dunning says.

In 1867 Bureau officers took part in the registration of Black voters under the Military Reconstruction Acts; in some places a Bureau agent was in charge of registering voters alongside his Bureau duties, even though the army commanders held the legal authority. Southern whites who watched federal Bureau agents enrolling freedmen as voters could see the Bureau as a device for national control of the South, which is what Dunning describes.

Congress's 1867 Reconstruction legislation, enforced by army commanders, brought Bureau agents into the supervision of the elections for the constitutional conventions, where they helped freedmen register and protected them from intimidation. Because the Bureau was thus tied to Black voting under federal authority, white Southerners could read it as the national government's instrument of control, as Dunning claims.
Generals Steedman and Fullerton inspected the Bureau in 1866.
White Southerners hated the Bureau and some of its agents were oppressive, which supports Dunning because he says the same thing.

In 1867 the Freedmen's Bureau alone ran every Southern election and decided who could vote, replacing the army commanders, and this control by federal agents supports Dunning's view that the Bureau was an instrument of national control.
The Ku Klux Klan terrorized Black voters in 1920s Alabama, which shows white hostility to Black political rights and so supports Dunning.

In late 1865 Mississippi and South Carolina passed Black Codes that required freed workers to hold yearly written labor contracts and punished those without lawful employment as vagrants. These laws threatened the economic and civil rights that Du Bois says the Bureau was trying to protect, so they show the need for the Bureau's protection.

In 1865 and 1866 President Johnson's pardons led to most of the land that Sherman's Field Order No. 15 had set aside for freed families, including on Edisto Island, being returned to former owners. The national government's withdrawal of support for freed families' land supports Du Bois's point that the Bureau's task was repudiated.

In October 1865 Commissioner Howard went to Edisto Island and told freed families that Johnson's pardons meant the land they had settled would go back to its former owners. Although some Bureau officials were unhappy with the policy, the Bureau carried it out, and freed people there petitioned against it. The reversal of land policy by the national government supports Du Bois's claim that the Bureau's work was repudiated.

In late 1865 freedpeople on Edisto Island sent President Johnson a petition saying 'this is our home' and asking that their land not be returned to its former Confederate owners, but the land was restored to the planters. Because the Bureau, charged with protecting freed people's economic rights, saw its land policy reversed by the president, this supports Du Bois's statement that its task was repudiated.
The Freedmen's Bureau founded Fisk University by itself in 1866, which shows the great task it accomplished, as Du Bois says.
The Freedmen's Bureau as an agency refused to return the land on Edisto Island and blocked Johnson's pardons in 1865, which shows it protected freed people and so supports Du Bois.
Bureau agents were teachers who educated freed people, which supports Du Bois because he says so himself.
The 1954 Brown v. Board of Education decision ended school segregation, which shows the Bureau's protection of freed people's rights, supporting Du Bois.
